name: Triple Attack
description: Zeus is analyzing a replay of the fight to understand his opponent's attack patterns. The opponent has a special ability: if they land three attacks on a target within a time frame of $$$z$$$, their third attack becomes a powerful, boosted attack. To outplay his opponent, Zeus should not let his opponent trigger their boosted attack. Let $$$Y = \{y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m\}$$$ be the multiset of $$$m$$$ timestamps, where each $$$y_i$$$ represents the time when the opponent's attack landed. We call $$$Y$$$ to be safe if for every three timestamps $$$\{y_i, y_j, y_k\}$$$ such that $$$1 \le i \lt j \lt k \le m$$$, it holds that $$$\max(y_i, y_j, y_k) - \min(y_i, y_j, y_k) \gt z$$$, where $$$z$$$ is the duration of the time frame that is given to you as an input. Zeus has a log of $$$n$$$ timestamps, $$$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$$$, representing when the opponent's attacks landed. The timestamps are sorted in nondecreasing order of occurrence. In other words, $$$x_i \le x_{i+1}$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \lt n$$$. Zeus has $$$q$$$ intervals of interest, denoted as two integers $$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$. For each interval, Zeus wants to find the maximum number of attacks among $$$[x_l, x_{l+1}, \ldots, x_r]$$$ that he could have let through: In other words, Zeus wants to find a maximum size subset of the multiset $$$\{x_l, x_{l+1}, \ldots, x_r\}$$$ such that the subset is safe .
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 20\,000$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$z$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 250\,000$$$, $$$1 \le z \le 10^9$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i \le 10^9$$$) — the timestamps of the opponent's attacks. It is guaranteed that the array $$$x$$$ is sorted, i.e., $$$x_i \le x_{i+1}$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \lt n$$$. The third line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 250\,000$$$). The next $$$q$$$ lines each contain two integers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$) — the endpoints of the interval. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$250\,000$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$250\,000$$$.
output_specification: For each of the $$$q$$$ queries, print a single integer — the maximum size of a safe subset of attack timestamps in the given interval.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2152F — Triple Attack [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
